observations.evidence: Hung on bent arms while static for 16 s total
observations.drill: Practice 'lock-off' drills where you lock your arms straight for 10 seconds before moving, forcing you to rely on your lats rather than biceps.

observations.evidence: Foot contact broke down (toes pitched off the hold) in 4 stretches
observations.drill: Perform 'silent feet' practice where you must place your foot without making a sound to ensure full surface area contact before weighting it.

observations.evidence: Hips sagged below the starting baseline for 1 s total
Hips swung out and back on 1 move
Full-crimp grip geometry on 12 sampled frames
observations.drill: Practice 'open hand' hangs on large edges to train your forearms to support your weight without bending the top joint of your fingers.

coaching_text:
You are showing great commitment to the problem, but your efficiency is being drained by static tension. The analysis highlights significant 'bent arm hangs' and 'poor foot contact,' which are directly visible in the evidence frames. You are relying heavily on arm strength to hold positions rather than using your body position to rest. 

Looking at the context, your climbing style is currently very static, but you are not utilizing it effectively; you are hanging off the wall rather than pressing into it. Your hips are often too far away from the wall, which forces your arms to bend and your feet to slip. To fix this, you need to focus on 'hip drive.' When you reach for a hold, actively push your hips toward the wall to straighten your arms. This simple shift will offload your shoulders and allow your feet to stay planted. 

The 'full crimp' detection is also a valid concern given the volume of crimping on this route. Focus on transitioning to open-hand grips on the larger volumes to save your finger strength for the crux. Trust your feet more—place them precisely and push through them to keep your arms straight. This will turn a V4 struggle into a controlled climb.
